title: How to make a great portfolio
summary: A practical way to show machining, automation and electronics work without pretending to know more than you do.

blocks.title: Make the work easy to see
blocks.body: A good portfolio is not a trophy case. It is a clean handoff: what you worked on, how you thought, what changed, and what you would check next. One honest, well-explained job beats a pile of vague claims.

blocks.heading: The goal
blocks.body: Give a hiring manager, lead, customer or collaborator enough evidence to understand how you work. They should be able to tell what you can already do, what you understand well enough to explain, and what you are still learning. Keep those three things separate. That is not underselling yourself. It is good labeling.

blocks.heading: Label every claim
rows: DONE
Work you personally completed or helped complete
Your role, the evidence, the result and any limits
UNDERSTANDS
Ideas you can explain and apply, even if you did not own the full job
A clear explanation, a small example and the boundary of your experience
LEARNING
Skills you are actively building
A lab, course, test, question log or next experiment
blocks.caption: If a sentence cannot be labeled cleanly, rewrite it until it can.

items.label: One real piece of work
items.detail: A setup improvement, troubleshooting path, PLC exercise, circuit test, fixture, safety lesson or build. Start small and real.

items.label: Evidence you are allowed to share
items.detail: Photos, sketches, redrawn diagrams, measurements, code excerpts or a simple recreation. Remove company names, customer data, credentials, serial numbers and anything covered by policy.

items.label: A short work log
items.detail: Write down the starting condition, your part, the checks you made, the result and the open questions while you still remember them.

items.label: A plain place to publish
items.detail: A simple site or PDF is enough. Clear pages matter more than fancy effects.

nodes.title: Pick
nodes.detail: Choose one small piece of work with evidence.

nodes.title: Build
nodes.detail: Turn the work into a short case page.

nodes.title: Check
nodes.detail: Verify facts, permissions, links and readability.

nodes.title: Publish
nodes.detail: Share it, then improve it when the work earns an update.

blocks.heading: Build the first page
items: Name the situation in one sentence. What machine, process, signal or problem was in front of you?
State your part. Say what you owned, what you helped with and what belonged to someone else.
Show the evidence. Use a photo, diagram, reading, code excerpt or test result, then explain what the reader is looking at.
Walk through the reasoning. Record the useful checks in order, including the checks that ruled something out.
State the result without stretching it. Say what changed, what did not change and how you verified it.
End with what you understand now and what you are learning next.

blocks.heading: A case page that stays readable

slides.title: 1. Situation
slides.body: Two or three sentences: the equipment or project, the symptom or goal, and the boundary you were working inside.

slides.title: 2. Your part
slides.body: Use direct verbs. I measured. I machined. I wired. I changed. I observed. I helped test. Do not borrow the whole team's work.

slides.title: 3. Evidence
slides.body: Put the useful image, sketch, trend, reading or code close to the sentence that explains it. Caption what matters.

slides.title: 4. Reasoning
slides.body: Show the path from signal to check to conclusion. The reader does not need every detour, just enough to trust the path.

slides.title: 5. Result
slides.body: Say how you checked the outcome. If the result was partial, call it partial.

slides.title: 6. Next
slides.body: Name the remaining risk, next test or skill you are learning. An honest edge makes the finished work stronger, not weaker.

blocks.heading: Turn a weak claim into useful evidence

columns.name: Before
columns.detail: Experienced with PLC troubleshooting and industrial automation.

columns.name: After
columns.detail: DONE: traced an intermittent photoeye input to a loose field connection, replaced the terminal and verified ten clean cycles. UNDERSTANDS: how the input state moved through the PLC logic. LEARNING: better ways to capture intermittent faults over longer runs.

items.label: A stranger can explain your part
items.detail: Ask them what you did after a two-minute skim. If they give you the team's result instead, tighten the ownership language.

items.label: Every strong claim has nearby evidence
items.detail: The photo, reading, drawing, code or result should support the sentence, not just decorate the page.

items.label: DONE, UNDERSTANDS and LEARNING do not blur together
items.detail: The reader should never have to guess whether you performed the work, understand the idea or are exploring it.

items.label: The page works on a phone
items.detail: Check type size, image captions, tables, links and the first screen. A busy reader should not need to pinch and hunt.

items.label: Nothing private slipped through
items.detail: Recheck backgrounds, screens, filenames, badges, serial plates, drawings and metadata before publishing.

blocks.heading: Mistakes to avoid
rows: Listing tools with no work attached
The reader cannot see how you used them
Connect each important tool to one case or exercise
Writing like a brochure
Big words hide the work
Use shop-floor language and specific verbs
Taking credit for the whole job
It makes every other claim harder to trust
Name your part and the team boundary
Only showing the polished result
The reasoning stays invisible
Show the useful evidence trail
Hiding unfinished learning
It forces you to bluff or stay silent
Label LEARNING and show the next real step
Publishing sensitive details
A portfolio is never worth breaking trust or policy
Redraw, crop, anonymize or leave it out
Waiting for a perfect website
The work never gets shown
Publish one clear page, then add the next

blocks.title: A good first week
blocks.body: Pick one real example. Gather only the evidence you may share. Write the six-part case page. Ask one person to skim it. Fix what they misunderstood. Publish. That is a portfolio now; the next page makes it better.

blocks.heading: Start with one honest page
blocks.body: Use a job you can explain without guessing. Label what is DONE, what you UNDERSTAND and what you are LEARNING. Make the evidence easy to inspect. Then stop polishing and ship the page.
